title: Transverse quantum-state characterization of programmable electron optics
authors: Shengbo You, Paolo Rosi, Enzo Rotunno, Alberto Roncaglia, Luca Belsito, Amir H. Tavabi, Rafal E. Dunin-Borkowski, Vincenzo Grillo, Philipp M. Pelz
abstract: Programmable electron optics -- electronically controlled phase plates -- underpin proposals from dose-efficient phase imaging to shaped-electron X-ray sources, nearly all assuming a pure, fully coherent delivered wave whose purity has never been measured. Here we reconstruct the transverse density matrix of a microelectromechanical electrostatic spiral phase plate by mixed-state ptychography, from one four-dimensional STEM scan per state and without added hardware. The delivered beam is substantially mixed: its purity falls from approximately 0.47 to approximately 0.24 as the applied bias grows, inconsistent with a fixed lateral source-blur model, while the real-space coherence width stays near 1 nm. The same scans calibrate the device in situ, allow virtual orbital-angular-momentum sorting and, through a partial-coherence-aware transfer theory, indicate that purifying the output could improve dose efficiency roughly threefold. One acquisition thus becomes a quantum-state acceptance test for programmable electron optics, supplying the purity and coherence that emerging phase-plate and diffractive-imaging schemes assume but leave unquantified.
summary: The researchers characterized the quantum state of electron beams generated by programmable electrostatic phase plates using mixed-state ptychography. They found that the delivered beam is significantly mixed, contradicting idealized assumptions used in current imaging proposals. This work provides essential, quantitative measurements of beam purity and coherence for next-generation electron optics.
main_problem: The core problem is that proposals for advanced electron microscopy techniques rely on assuming the delivered electron wave is pure and fully coherent, a property that has never been quantitatively measured.
main_result: The study successfully reconstructed the transverse density matrix of an electrostatic spiral phase plate, revealing that the delivered beam is substantially mixed, with purity dropping significantly as the applied bias increases.
method: Mixed-state ptychography was employed using standard 4D STEM scans to reconstruct the full transverse density matrix ($ho$) for various programmed charge states.
model_or_system: The physical system is a microelectromechanical electrostatic spiral phase plate (SPP) used to generate and control electron vortex beams with tunable Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM). The analysis models the beam state using its density matrix formalism.
key_observables: Transverse density matrix ($ho$), purity ($	ext{Tr} ho^2$), von Neumann entropy ($S$), mode powers, and spatial coherence as functions of applied bias/charge.
important_parameters: The measured purity drops from $\approx 0.47$ to $\approx 0.24$ with increasing bias; the reconstructed OAM ($\langle\ellangle$) scales linearly with voltage.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation is that current diagnostics only measure diagonal elements or assume pure states, and the reconstruction technique itself relies on specific modeling assumptions regarding coherence transfer.
figures_summary: Figures show reconstructed probe modes in real space (annular intensity) and aperture plane (azimuthal winding); spectra track mode power, purity, and entropy as a function of programmed charge; one figure shows the linear calibration of mean OAM vs. voltage.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the gap by noting unmeasured beam purity. It then details the mixed-state ptychography method applied to the SPP. Results quantify the state mixing and coherence for multiple vortex states, concluding with implications for dose efficiency improvements.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial quantum characterization of an electron source used in advanced imaging, directly addressing the necessary input parameters (purity/coherence) that theoretical models often assume but fail to quantify experimentally.
